paras: The attempted lynching of W. H. Yeatts was an effort by a mounted, armed mob to take the condemned murderer Walter Hamilton Yeatts from the jail at Chatham, Pittsylvania County, Virginia, and hang him early on Saturday, July 29, 1882. The party, numbered at between sixty-five and a hundred men, dispersed without attacking the jail, and Yeatts was legally hanged at Chatham a week later. Yeatts was white, and the papers treated the episode as a sequel to a much-followed Virginia murder case.

Yeatts, the 26-year-old son of Major Charles W. Yeatts, a former internal-revenue collector at Lynchburg, was convicted of killing Presley E. Adkerson, a young merchant and depot master at Sycamore station, in February 1882. According to the Richmond Dispatch, citizens of the neighborhood had already made threats and some preparations to lynch him when he was brought back to the Chatham jail after his arrest at Bristol. Sentenced at the May term of the County Court to hang on July 28, he received a one-week respite from Governor Cameron while the governor examined new affidavits submitted by his father.
A Chatham correspondent wrote that county sentiment had turned "decidedly against the prisoner," while the father's counsel, D. H. Pannill, pointed to petitions signed in Yeatts's behalf.

A special telegram to the Dispatch reported that between seventy-five and a hundred armed men came to Chatham about 3 o'clock that morning to take Yeatts from the jail and hang him to a tree, having heard that the governor had commuted his sentence. A special to the Richmond Whig put the party at seventy-five horsemen "armed to the teeth" from the neighborhood of the murder, who came within half a mile of town. Both Chatham dispatches said the men gave up when they learned that Yeatts had only been respited; the Dispatch named Adkerson's stepfather, Mr. Simpson, as the man who told them.

Wire accounts gave a different reason: scouts sent ahead found the jail lighted and guarded and officials watchful, and the party, expecting determined resistance, retired and dispersed. No one was hurt, and no report of arrests of the mob's members appears in the coverage.

The governor decided not to interfere, and Sheriff Overby hanged Yeatts in a private execution behind the Chatham courthouse on August 4, 1882. The Dispatch printed a verse Yeatts wrote after being told of the night riders, which began "Aroused from slumber by the tread of horses."

The Richmond Dispatch broke the story on July 30 under the headline "Lynchers After Yeatts," and the Alexandria Gazette, Staunton Spectator and Valley Virginian reprinted its paragraph, with the stepfather's name varying between Simpson and Sampson. The Washington National Republican reprinted the Whig's version on August 3.

Outside Virginia, the New-York Tribune and a Lancaster, Pennsylvania, news roundup carried the guarded-jail version, the Intelligencer calling the mob "the would-be butchers." Weeklies in Tennessee and Pennsylvania ran a shorter wire summary into late August that credited "the watchfulness of officials" and repeated the claim that the respite rested on the bride's alleged intimacy with Adkerson. No paper in the coverage commented on the mob in an editorial, and the race of the condemned man was stated only after his execution, by the Savannah Morning News.

The size of the mob was given as about sixty-five in the wire accounts, seventy-five in the Whig special and seventy-five to a hundred in the Dispatch telegram. Most accounts placed the approach at about 3 o'clock in the morning, while the reprinted Whig special gave about 8 o'clock.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of W. H. Yeatts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An armed mounted mob came to the Chatham jail to take a condemned prisoner out and hang him, then dispersed without attacking (A1, A3, A7); the target was a white man (A13), so the episode is not anti-Black violence.

A mob of 65 to 100 men set out to hang Yeatts for the murder of which he had been convicted, but dispersed without seizing or harming him (A1, A3, A7); he was legally hanged a week later (A11), so no one was killed by the mob.

A Dispatch special telegram (A1), a Richmond Whig special (A7) and a separate wire account (A2, A3) agree that an armed mounted party came to Chatham to lynch Yeatts and dispersed, and Yeatts's own verse refers to it (A11).
